# Applications and outcomes of virtual reality in inpatient psychiatry: A systematic review

Zachary Fontaine-Dussault1, Lori Hazel2 , Logane Dupont3 , Clayton Jeffrey4 ,

Carolane Bernard-Gilbert2, Florence Fontaine2, Christina Soucy2, Michelle Wang4 ,

Martin Lepage3 and Elisabeth Thibaudeau2

1Universite de Montreal, Canada; 2Universite Laval Faculte des sciences sociales, Canada; 3Douglas Hospital Centre: Institut universitaire en sante mentale Douglas, Canada and 4McGill University Department of Psychology, Canada

Abstract

Background. Virtual reality (VR) has been widely used in outpatient psychiatric services and has demonstrated benefits across several clinical diagnoses, but its use and effects in inpatient settings remain to be explored. This systematic review aimed to examine the use of VR during psychiatric hospitalization, including types of VR applications, barriers and facilitators of implementation, and effects on various outcomes. Methods. The review was registered in PROSPERO (#CRD42023446524). Following PRISMA guidelines, databases (Ovid, SciVerse, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, ProQuest, and WorldCat) were searched from 1983 to 2025 using keywords related to VR and psychiatric disorders. Studies involving the use of VR with psychiatric inpatients (≥85%) were included. Descriptive statistics and narrative syntheses were used to summarize findings. Study quality was assessed with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Results. After full-text screening, 37 studies (N = 1,004) met inclusion criteria. VR was used for both assessment and intervention, with cognitive-behavioral therapy/exposure (35%) and assessment (24%) being the most frequently used. VR use in inpatient units appeared feasible, acceptable, and safe for inpatients and clinicians, though findings remain preliminary. Several facilitators (e.g. adequate staff training and supervision) and common barriers (e.g. technical difficulties and limited resources) were identified. The most consistent improvements were observed in clinical symptoms (e.g. anxiety) compared with psychosocial, cognitive, and physiological outcomes. Conclusions. These findings suggest that inpatient settings represent a promising, yet understudied context for VR-based assessments and interventions. High-quality trials and systematic reporting of implementation are needed in future studies to inform research and clinical practice.

Introduction

Virtual reality (VR) delivers immersive, multisensory environments via head-mounted displays, providing safe and controlled simulations that enhance engagement through interactive and gamified experiences. VR has demonstrated potential across diverse therapeutic applications in psychiatry (Freeman et al., 2017; Maples-Keller, Bunnell, Kim, & Rothbaum, 2017; Riva, Malighetti, & Serino, 2021). Previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have reported that immersive VR interventions may improve clinical outcomes across psychiatric disorders and are generally feasible and acceptable (Carl et al., 2019; Fodor et al., 2018; Maples-Keller et al., 2017; Valmaggia, Latif, Kempton, & Rus-Calafell, 2016; Zeka et al., 2025). However, these reviews have primarily focused on outpatient populations or psychiatric disorders broadly, providing limited insight into the implementation, feasibility, and effectiveness of VR in psychiatric inpatient settings. Although psychiatric inpatient care primarily emphasizes pharmacological stabilization (Alzahrani, 2021), psychosocial interventions targeting key recovery processes such as social connectedness, emotional regulation, and coping may further support personal recovery (Clemmensen et al., 2023; Dupont et al., 2026; Roe & Ronen, 2003). Their implementation is often limited by cost, resource constraints, and difficulties with personalization (Clemmensen et al., 2023). VR may help address these barriers by providing engaging, adaptable, and scalable recovery-oriented interventions as an adjunct to usual care (Clemmensen et al., 2023). Inpatient settings represent a unique clinical context in which VR may encounter distinct barriers, facilitators, and outcomes (Alzahrani, 2021; Dupont et al., 2026; Roe & Ronen, 2003). Hospitalized individuals often present with acute symptom exacerbations, severe functional impairment, or elevated distress requiring intensive care (Alzahrani, 2021; Roe & Ronen, 2003).

Many are also admitted involuntarily or experience coercive practices, reduced autonomy, and restricted access to stimulating environments, all of which may influence engagement in psychosocial interventions and recovery (Clemmensen et al., 2023; Dupont et al., 2026). At the organizational level, implementation is shaped by short lengths of stay, high patient turnover, staffing and space constraints, and competing clinical priorities (Dupont et al., 2026; Riches et al., 2023; Waldemar, Esbensen, Korsbek, Petersen, & Arnfred, 2018). Conversely, inpatient care also offers unique opportunities for VR implementation, including continuous clinical supervision, structured daily routines, intensive intervention schedules, and close monitoring of treatment response and safety (Raphael et al., 2021). These contextual characteristics are likely to influence not only the feasibility of VR interventions, but also the types of interventions delivered and the outcomes achieved. A clearer understanding of VR use in psychiatric inpatient settings is therefore needed to guide evidence-based implementation and identify interventions most likely to benefit hospitalized individuals. This systematic review aimed to (1) characterize VR use in psychiatric inpatient settings, (2) document barriers and facilitators to implementation, and (3) evaluate outcomes in these settings.

Methodology

A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines (Page et al., 2021) (PROSPERO #CRD42023446524). Relevant references were identified through searches of Ovid, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, WorldCat, ProQuest, and OpenGrey. The search covered publications from 1983 to 2025, beginning with the publication of the DSM-III and the emergence of contemporary VR systems. Keywords related to psychiatric disorders and VR were used (see Supplementary Material S1). Bibliographies of included studies, systematic reviews, and metaanalyses were also examined. Studies were included if participants were psychiatric inpatients or if at least 85% of the sample consisted of psychiatric inpatients. Detailed eligibility criteria are presented in Table 1. All references were imported into Covidence for double-blind screening. Two independent reviewers screened each article at the title/abstract and full-text stages. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer involved if needed. Corresponding authors were contacted for missing information relevant to eligibility. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) (Hong et al., 2018), following the same independent review process. Data were extracted using a pre-developed Excel template, pilot-tested on five articles. Extracted information (Supplementary Material S2) included study and participant characteristics, VR use details, implementation variables, and outcomes. For the first objective, VR applications were categorized based on their primary purpose: relaxation and mindfulness, social skills training, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and exposure, cognitive training, and assessment. For the second objective, implementation outcomes were classified as feasibility, acceptability, and safety. For the third objective, all reported outcomes were extracted and subsequently grouped into four domains: clinical, psychosocial, cognitive, and physiological. Clinical outcomes referred to psychiatric symptoms. Psychosocial outcomes included functioning, self-efficacy, self-esteem, readiness to change, and general well-being. Cognitive outcomes encompassed both neurocognitive (e.g. memory) and social

cognitive domains (e.g. emotion recognition). Physiological outcomes included autonomic stress markers (e.g. heart rate) as well as body-related outcomes such as body mass index. Descriptive statistics and summary tables supported a narrative synthesis for all three objectives.

Results

After removing duplicates, 4,284 references were identified. Title and abstract screening yielded 819 articles. Following the full-text review, 782 studies were excluded, resulting in 37 studies being included (Figure 1). Findings are presented by objective, with higher-quality evidence discussed first, followed by nonrandomized studies, pilot studies, and qualitative studies. The PRISMA checklist is provided in Supplementary Material S3, and mixed inpatient/outpatient studies excluded from the synthesis are summarized in Supplementary Material S4.

Study characteristics

The 37 studies included 1,004 participants; characteristics are summarized in Table 2. Six diagnostic categories were identified: schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD [n = 12]), mixed psychiatric samples (n = 8), eating and food intake disorders (n = 8), substance use and addictive disorders (SUD [n = 6]), and mood disorders (n = 3). Methodological quality is summarized in Table 3, whereas VR applications and outcomes are summarized in Table 4.

Relaxation and mindfulness Seven studies used VR-based relaxation and mindfulness interventions. Two RCTs were identified. Lotfinia et al. (2024) compared VR environments to treatment as usual (TAU) for stress reduction in SUD. In a mixed psychiatric sample, Tan, Chng, Lau, and Klainin-Yobas (2021) assessed a VR-based stress management program.

Five nonrandomized studies extended this work by evaluating guided relaxation in SSD (Rault, Lamothe, & Pelissolo, 2022), VR compared with physical calm rooms (Ilioudi et al., 2023), and VR-based stress management (Shah et al., 2015) in mood disorders, as well as VR relaxation and mindfulness interventions in mixed psychiatric samples (Riches et al., 2023; Van Doren, Ng, Rawat, McKenna, & Blonigen, 2024).

Social skills training Four studies examined VR-based social skills interventions, including two RCTs. Park et al. (2011) examined VR role-playing integrated into social skills training in SSD, and Klein Tuente et al. (2020) assessed VR aggression prevention training in forensic psychiatry. A mixed-methods single-arm study evaluated therapist-guided VR role-plays integrated into psychodynamic psychotherapy in mood disorders (Holsteg et al., 2024), while a qualitative study explored patient experiences with VR-assisted aggression prevention training in a mixed psychiatric sample (González Moraga et al., 2024).

CBT and exposure therapy Thirteen studies examined VR-based CBT and exposure interventions. Five RCTs evaluated VR as an adjunct to inpatient psychotherapy, including four in eating disorders examining VR-enhanced CBT and exposure (Cesa et al., 2013; Porras-García et al., 2020; Riva, Bacchetta, Baruffi, & Molinari, 2002; Riva, Bacchetta, Cesa, Conti, & Molinari, 2003), and one in gambling disorder integrating VR into inpatient CBT (Bouchard et al., 2017). Six nonrandomized studies extended these findings to eating disorders, SUD, SSD with comorbid social anxiety, and mixed psychiatric samples, primarily evaluating the feasibility and preliminary effects of VR-enhanced CBT and exposure interventions (Greenwald et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2009; McLachlan, Mehdikhani, Larham, & Centifanti, 2022; Paslakis et al., 2017; Riva et al., 2000; Stefaniak & Aleksandrowicz, 2024). Two qualitative studies examined the implementation of VR-CBT in routine psychiatric care, including one study in SUD (Borelle & Forner, 2024) and another assessing the acceptability of automated VR cognitive therapy in a mixed psychiatric sample (Brown et al., 2022).

Objective 2: Barriers and facilitators

Across study designs, VR was generally feasible, acceptable, and safe for use in psychiatric inpatient settings. However, evidence primarily originated from pilot and feasibility studies, and implementation outcomes were reported inconsistently.

Feasibility Available evidence suggests that VR can be successfully implemented across psychiatric inpatient settings, with barriers mostly related to organizational factors. Common challenges included early discharge, short lengths of stay, limited availability of private spaces, competing clinical priorities, staff workload, technical difficulties, and, in some studies, COVID-19 disruptions (Brown et al., 2022; Holsteg et al., 2024; Komemi et al., 2024; Riches et al., 2023). Clinicians also emphasized the importance of staff training, technical support, and flexible scheduling (Brown et al., 2022; Holsteg et al., 2024; Riches et al., 2023). Technical specifications of VR systems are presented in Supplementary Material S5. Despite these challenges, reported implementation indicators were encouraging. Greenwald et al. (2024) reported that 33 of 62 eligible patients (53%) enrolled in an inpatient opioid withdrawal program, and completion rates were higher in the VR group than in the TAU group (63% vs. 45%), with discontinuations primarily related to medical care or discharge rather than the intervention. Similarly, Komemi et al. (2024) reported completion of an 8-session VR cognitive remediation program by 23 of 31 participants (74%), with most attrition attributable to early discharge. Across the remaining studies, authors consistently concluded that VR could be integrated into inpatient psychiatric care when adequate organizational support and technical resources were available (Ilioudi et al., 2023; Rault et al., 2022; Stefaniak & Aleksandrowicz, 2024; Tan et al., 2021; Van Doren et al., 2024).

Acceptability Acceptability was consistently high across RCTs (Ilioudi et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022), nonrandomized studies (Greenwald et al., 2024; Van Doren et al., 2024), and qualitative or mixed-methods studies (Brown et al., 2022; Holsteg et al., 2024; Riches et al., 2023). Participants described VR as engaging, immersive, enjoyable, and clinically meaningful, while facilitating relaxation, motivation, emotional engagement, and realistic yet safe opportunities to practice social interactions, emotion regulation, exposure, and everyday activities (Brown et al., 2022; Ilioudi et al., 2023; Just, Lütt, Siegle, &

Döring-Brandl, 2024; McLachlan et al., 2022; Park, Kim, Ku, et al., 2009; Riches et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2021). Quantitative findings supported these observations: 94% of participants in Greenwald et al. (2024) reported satisfaction with VR, while Van Doren et al. (2024) found high ratings of satisfaction, usability, presence, confidence, and mindfulness. Similarly, Park et al. (2011) reported greater treatment interest and better generalization of social skills, and Shen et al. (2022) observed higher adherence with VR-based SCIT than with traditional SCIT. Clinicians also viewed VR positively, highlighting its value for enhancing engagement and experiential learning (Bouchard et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2022; Holsteg et al., 2024; Riches et al., 2023; Van Doren et al., 2024). However, successful implementation depended on adequate staff training, technical support, and organizational readiness. Reported challenges included technical glitches, interruptions during role-plays, equipment maintenance, privacy considerations, and integration into routine unit activities (Brown et al., 2022; Holsteg et al., 2024; Riches et al., 2023).

Safety VR was generally well tolerated across psychiatric inpatient populations, and no study reported serious adverse events directly attributable to VR. When assessed, cybersickness was uncommon and typically mild and transient, consisting primarily of headaches, dizziness, eye irritation, headset discomfort, or temporary distress (Li et al., 2022; Riches et al., 2023). Likewise, studies evaluating VR relaxation (Rault et al., 2022), CBT and exposure (Riva et al., 2000; Riva et al., 2002; Stefaniak & Aleksandrowicz, 2024), stress management (Shah et al., 2015), mindfulness (Van Doren et al., 2024), and opioid withdrawal (Greenwald et al., 2024) reported no major safety concerns. Although several interventions intentionally elicited anxiety, craving, body-related distress, or aggressive impulses as part of therapeutic exposure, these reactions occurred within the expected therapeutic framework and were not associated with unexpected adverse events (Klein Tuente et al., 2020; Paslakis et al., 2017; Porras-García et al., 2020). Similarly, Park, Kim, Ku, et al. (2009) reported transient increases in social anxiety during VR-based social interactions in SSD, but concluded that responses reflected the emotional content of the stimuli rather than the VR technology itself. A few studies reported emotional overload or suggested that VR was unsuitable for patients who were too acutely unwell or perceived the intervention as irrelevant (Brown et al., 2022; Holsteg et al., 2024; Riches et al., 2023). Overall, reported safety concerns were primarily related to the therapeutic content and patient selection rather than to the VR technology.

Objective 3: Treatment outcomes

Clinical symptoms Higher-quality evidence from RCTs suggests mixed but generally promising effects of VR-based interventions on clinical symptoms across psychiatric diagnoses. Lower-level evidence from nonrandomized and mixed-methods studies was generally consistent with these findings. Regarding VR-based relaxation and mindfulness, results from an RCT comparing VR-based relaxation/mindfulness with waitlist controls in a mixed psychiatric sample showed improved perceived relaxation and stress-management knowledge, with large effect sizes (Tan et al., 2021 [N = 40]). The results were supported by mixed-methods studies reporting large improvements in relaxation, stress, anxiety, and sadness (Riches et al., 2023 [N = 28]),

Finally, a single-arm study in binge-eating disorder reported reductions in binge eating together with improvements in body-related outcomes following VR-based experiential cognitive therapy (Riva et al., 2000 [N = 25]). Likewise, preliminary RCTs in gambling disorder found reductions in gambling cravings comparable with standard CBT (Bouchard et al., 2017) (Study 2, N = 20; Study 3, N = 14). In SUD, VR interventions reduced craving and negative affect, with one pilot study reporting large improvements in depressive symptoms, tension, and craving following repeated exposure to naturalistic VR environments (Greenwald et al., 2024 [N = 32]) and another showing greater reductions in alcohol craving than conventional CBT in alcohol use disorder (Lee et al., 2009 [N = 20]). In mixed psychiatric samples, McLachlan et al. (2022 [N = 29]) reported moderate-to-large improvements in beliefs regarding the malleability of emotions following a brief VR-based psychoeducational intervention. In SSD, VR-CBT reduced symptom severity, social anxiety, and depressive symptoms compared to TAU (Stefaniak & Aleksandrowicz, 2024 [N = 11]) in a nonrandomized study. Regarding social skills training, VR-assisted aggression prevention therapy produced small-to-moderate improvements in anger control, impulsiveness, and hostility in forensic psychiatry, although effects on primary aggression outcomes were negligible and were not maintained at 3-month follow-up (Klein Tuente et al., 2020 [N = 64]).

Psychosocial outcomes Higher-quality evidence from RCTs suggests that VR interventions may improve psychosocial functioning across several psychiatric populations. Regarding VR-based relaxation and mindfulness, Ilioudi et al. (2023 [N = 40]) found no significant differences in well-being when comparing a VR calm room with a physical calm room in mood disorders, although both interventions produced moderate-to-large

within-group improvements. A mixed-methods study in a mixed psychiatric sample reported large improvements in happiness, relaxation, and connectedness to nature following immersive naturebased VR (Riches et al., 2023 [N = 28]). Regarding CBT, two RCTs in eating disorders showed improvements in self-efficacy, readiness to change, and self-esteem compared with TAU, conventional CBT, or waitlist controls (Riva et al., 2002 [N = 20]; Riva et al., 2003 [N = 36]). A single-arm study in binge-eating disorder also reported reduced social avoidance and greater social engagement following VR-based experiential cognitive therapy (Riva et al., 2000 [N = 25]). In SSD, VR-based CBT improved global functioning but did not reduce internalized stigma (Stefaniak & Aleksandrowicz, 2024 [N = 11]). Regarding social skills training, one RCT in SSD showed that VR-assisted social skills training improved conversational ability and assertiveness compared with an active control group (Park et al., 2011 [N = 33]). Regarding cognitive remediation, a single-arm study found that ecological VR-based cognitive remediation improved functional capacity and participation in everyday activities (Komemi et al., 2024 [N = 23]).

Cognitive outcomes Higher-quality evidence from RCTs suggests that VR interventions improve both neurocognition and social cognition in SSD. VR-based cognitive training was associated with improvements in visual learning and reasoning/problem-solving, with a large overall treatment effect compared with TAU (Li et al., 2022 [N = 62]). Similarly, Wang et al. (2022 [N = 31]) reported moderate-to-large improvements in executive functioning and working memory following a VR serious game intervention compared with TAU. Additional evidence from an RCT supports the use of VR to target social cognition. Shen et al. (2022 [N = 26]) found that VR-based SCIT improved emotion recognition, theory of mind, metacognition, and social functioning while reducing hostile attribution bias compared with traditional SCIT and a waiting-list control. Consistent preliminary evidence was provided in a single-arm study by Komemi et al. (2024 [n = 23]) who reported small-tomoderate improvements across several neurocognitive domains, including processing speed, cognitive flexibility, verbal fluency, and functional capacity following ecological VR-based cognitive remediation.

Physiological outcomes Higher-quality evidence from RCTs suggests that VR-based interventions may improve selected physiological outcomes, although findings remain limited. Discussion

This systematic review synthesized evidence regarding the use, feasibility, acceptability, safety, and effects of VR in psychiatric inpatient settings. Overall, findings indicate that VR has been applied across diverse psychiatric diagnoses and therapeutic contexts, including relaxation/mindfulness, social skills training, CBT/exposure, cognitive training, and assessment. These applications largely mirror those reported in outpatient settings (Freeman et al., 2017; Maples-Keller et al., 2017; Valmaggia et al., 2016). However, CBT/exposure and assessment accounted for most studies, reflecting the current stage of VR implementation in psychiatry (Benbow & Anderson, 2019; Carl et al., 2019; Fernández-Álvarez et al., 2019). Across studies, VR was associated with improvements in clinical, psychosocial, cognitive, and physiological outcomes and was generally feasible, acceptable, and safe for both inpatients and clinicians. Nevertheless, these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the substantial heterogeneity in VR modalities, psychiatric populations, intervention protocols, and methodological quality.

Benefits of VR-based treatments in inpatient settings

Overall, VR-based interventions demonstrated benefits across multiple outcome domains despite the greater clinical acuity typically encountered in inpatient settings. Clinical improvements were reported across SSD, mood disorders, eating disorders, SUD, and mixed psychiatric samples, while psychosocial benefits included enhanced interpersonal functioning, well-being, relaxation, and self-efficacy. These findings are consistent with previous outpatient-focused reviews (Carl et al., 2019; G. Riva, Wiederhold, & Mantovani, 2019; Wechsler, Kümpers, & Mühlberger, 2019) and the recent meta-analysis by Zeka et al. (2025), which concluded that VR interventions may benefit several psychiatric disorders while emphasizing that the certainty of the evidence remains low to moderate because of methodological limitations. The immersive and interactive characteristics of VR may partly explain these findings by promoting presence and facilitating safe engagement with avoided or emotionally salient stimuli(Riva et al., 2019). Such features may be particularly valuable in inpatient care, where emotional dysregulation, reduced motivation, and avoidance can limit participation in conventional psychosocial interventions (Clemmensen et al., 2023; Roe & Ronen, 2003). VR also showed promise for cognitive remediation in inpatient care. Consistent with the previous meta-analysis of inpatient cognitive remediation by Cella et al. (2020), RCTs demonstrated improvements in neurocognition and social cognition (Li et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022). Beyond improving cognitive functioning, VR may provide a more engaging and

ecologically valid platform for practicing cognitive and social cognitive skills than conventional approaches. Evidence for physiological effects was more limited, but suggests that VR may influence autonomic stress response alongside psychological outcomes (Lotfinia et al., 2024; Porras-García et al., 2020; Shah et al., 2015). However, the durability of these effects remains uncertain because most studies assessed only short-term outcomes and some benefits diminished at follow-up. Future studies should therefore examine post-discharge maintenance and long-term effects on functioning, symptoms, and quality of life. Although beneficial effects were observed across several diagnoses, evidence remains preliminary.

Feasibility, acceptability, and safety

Overall, VR interventions were found to be feasible, acceptable, and safe in psychiatric inpatient settings. Users reported high levels of satisfaction, realism, and engagement, and most completed the interventions. Reported dropout rates were low, which may have been supported by the gamification component of VR but also by the inpatient setting where structured routines and realtime monitoring facilitate adherence and individualized delivery (Balachander et al., 2020; Raphael et al., 2021). Further, successful implementation depended primarily on organizational factors rather than on the technology itself. Consistent with previous reviews (e.g. Maples-Keller et al., 2017), adequate staff training, technical support, and institutional readiness emerged as key facilitators, whereas limited staffing, technical difficulties, equipment maintenance, and restricted physical space represented the principal barriers (Raphael et al., 2021; Riva et al., 2019). These findings suggest that implementation efforts should focus as much on organizational readiness as on the technology itself. Although occasional emotional overload or transient symptom exacerbation was reported, these events should be interpreted within the therapeutic context of the interventions. Several VR applications intentionally incorporated exposure to anxietyprovoking, emotionally salient, or craving-related stimuli as part of evidence-based CBT/exposure. Consequently, temporary increases in distress or emotional activation likely reflect the expected therapeutic process rather than adverse effects of VR technology. The distinction may be particularly relevant in psychiatric inpatient settings, where patients often present with greater clinical instability than outpatient populations. Appropriate patient selection, clinician supervision, gradual exposure, and structured debriefing therefore remain essential to maximize therapeutic benefits while minimizing unnecessary distress (Maples-Keller et al., 2017; Riches et al., 2023).

Implications for implementation of VR in inpatient care

This review highlights several practical considerations for implementing VR in psychiatric inpatient care. First, clinician training and access to technical support appear essential for successful adoption. Second, user-friendly and clinically accessible VR applications may facilitate implementation by reducing technical complexity and staff burden. Third, staffing constraints remain an important challenge, although certain interventions, such as relaxation/mindfulness, and cognitive training may be delivered by nonspecialized staff following appropriate training, potentially improving feasibility and accessibility. Finally, future studies should clarify the influence of psychoactive medications and symptom severity on the safety and effectiveness of VR-based

Review strengths and limitations

This review followed PRISMA guidelines and included a comprehensive search of peer-reviewed and gray literature, reducing the risk ofpublication bias. Study qualitywas generally adequateaccordingto the MMAT. Another strength is the geographical diversity of the included studies. Although VR may be perceived as a technology used in high-income countries, several studies originated from diverse settings, including Brazil, China, and Iran, suggesting growing global interest in VR applications for psychiatric care. Several limitations should also be acknowledged. Inconsistent reporting of inpatient status and the absence of author responses resulted in the exclusion of potentially relevant studies. Excluding study protocols may also have omitted forthcoming evidence. Additionally, many studies included small and heterogeneous samples, and the diversity of interventions, outcomes, study designs, and psychiatric diagnoses precluded quantitative synthesis and limited direct comparisons across studies. Unlike broader metaanalyses (e.g. Zeka et al., 2025), this review specifically focused on psychiatric inpatient settings and therefore adopted a narrative synthesis to capture the diversity of interventions, implementation factors, and study designs. Publication bias also cannot be excluded, as studies with positive findings may have been more likely to be published. Finally, limited reporting of hospitalization duration prevented examination of how length of stay may influence VR implementation, dosage, or outcomes.

Conclusion

This review found that VR has been applied across a broad range of psychiatric inpatient settings and that available evidence generally supports its feasibility, acceptability, and safety while suggesting potential benefits across clinical, psychosocial, cognitive, and physiological outcomes. However, the current evidence remains preliminary because of small sample sizes, methodological heterogeneity, and limited long-term follow-up. VR therefore appears to represent a promising complement to, rather than a replacement for, conventional inpatient care. Future research should prioritize adequately powered trials, standardized intervention and safety procedures, and long-term follow-up to better define the role of VR in psychiatric inpatient practice.
